params.text:
Communication and de-escalation techniques

De-escalation is the set of skills you use to reduce agitation and help a person regain control. It depends far more on how you communicate than on what you say — research on face-to-face contact suggests that tone of voice and body language often carry more meaning than the words themselves, so a calm, respectful presence often does more than any single phrase.

  • Stay calm — control your own tone and breathing, and keep your voice low, slow and warm even if the person is loud. Your composure is contagious, and so is panic.
  • Listen actively — give the person your full attention, let them finish, and reflect back what you hear so they know they are being taken seriously.
  • Show empathy — acknowledge how they feel; feeling heard reduces the need to escalate.
  • Use non-threatening body language — stay open and relaxed with open hands, and avoid pointing, folded arms, staring or squaring up.
  • Give space — keep a respectful distance so the person does not feel cornered or crowded, and approach from the side rather than head-on.
  • Offer choices — restoring a sense of control helps a person feel less powerless.
  • Do not argue — avoid correcting, blaming, or trying to win; that only fuels the conflict.

The Betari Box

The Betari Box is a simple way to understand how attitudes and behaviour feed each other. It describes a loop: your attitude shapes your behaviour, your behaviour affects the other person’s attitude, and their attitude then shapes their behaviour back towards you.

In practice, if you approach someone feeling irritated, it leaks into your face and voice, they pick up on it and respond in kind, and the situation spirals. The good news is that the loop works both ways. By deliberately staying calm and respectful, you can help steady the other person — you are the part of the cycle you can always control.

params.alt: Two people sitting opposite each other having a calm, open conversation

params.question: The Betari Box suggests that if you change your own attitude and behaviour, you can influence how the other person responds to you.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. The Betari Box is about a two-way loop: changing your own attitude and behaviour genuinely influences how the other person responds.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Attitude and behaviour feed each other in a loop, so staying calm and respectful can help steady the other person — and your own response is the part you can control.

params.textField: Staying *calm* helps to defuse tension, because panic is contagious. Listen *actively* so the person feels genuinely heard. Show *empathy* by acknowledging how they feel. Give the person *space* so they do not feel cornered. Offer *choices* to restore their sense of control. Above all, do not *argue*, as trying to win only fuels the conflict.
